title: NCCL pacing and packetization impact on cross-node LLM inference
content:
Summary:
This is an investigation into a reproducible p99 latency spike and throughput variability we observed when serving decoder-only models across two nodes (4 GPUs total) using tensor+pipeline parallelism. Root cause appears correlated with small-payload NCCL traffic patterns and RDMA/TCP packetization behavior when KV-cache syncs are frequent and highly fragmented. This doc captures experiments, profiling artifacts, hypotheses, and proposed mitigations.

Context / Why this matters:
- Production serving traces from a mid-size customer show intermittent 2x p99 latency regressions when traffic mixes short (few-token) and long (streaming) requests.
- Problem surface: cross-node multi-GPU inference (tensor parallel with KV cache syncs at every new generation step) is sensitive to how NCCL breaks up messages, and to NIC-level segmentation/coalescing. Under worst combos we saw throughput fall ~30% and p99 increase by ~2x.

Testbed & topology:
- Two identical machines (node-A, node-B). Each: 2x A100-40GB GPUs, PCIe x16, NVLink between GPUs in-node. Mellanox ConnectX-6 DX NICs, RoCEv2 enabled, MTU set to 9000.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, OFED 5.6.x, NVIDIA driver 530.xx, NCCL 2.18.4, CUDA 12.1.
- Serving runtime: Redwood inference runtime branch: feature/kv-sync-pacing / PR 678.
- Workloads: 7B decoder-only model with tensor-parallel=2, pipeline-parallel=2, batch sizes vary (1, 4, 8 concurrent requests). Mixed request length distribution: 10% long (>512 tokens streaming), 70% short (<32 tokens), 20% medium.

Profiling tools used:
- nsight-systems (nsys) for kernel timelines and host<->device transfer timing.
- tcpdump + tshark to capture packet sizes and segmentation patterns.
- nvidia-smi nvlink stats for intra-node link utilization.
- ibv_devinfo / iblinkinfo for RoCE path checks.
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_TRACE=1 for internal op timelines.
- perf on host CPU for syscall hot spots.

Observations (high level):
1) Traffic pattern: KV-sync calls produce many small allgather/allreduce operations (sizes often < 8KB) at a high frequency (once per new token or per shard update). These small ops dominate cross-node RDMA traffic when many short requests are interleaved.
2) Packetization: NIC/driver (RoCE) was transmitting very small packets (often ~256B-1KB) due to fragmentation at the runtime layer and inability to coalesce back-to-back small DMA regions. Large headers + small payloads cause poor wire efficiency and high per-packet CPU/NIC overhead.
3) NIC offloads: TSO/GSO were not effective for these RDMA/UCX paths; GDRCopy path reduces CPU copies but didn't eliminate small-packet overhead.
4) NCCL behavior: Default algorithm and launch settings lead to a bursty sequence of many small network sends. NCCL internal pacing sometimes amplifies bursts (when multiple rings/trees run concurrently).
5) Measured impact: baseline (default config) for 4-GPU run: steady-state 230 tokens/sec, p99=220ms. With explicit pacing + coalescing (see experiments) improved to 310 tokens/sec, p99=140ms (approx +35% throughput, ~36% p99 reduction).

Key experiments & results:
A) MTU change (1500 -> 9000)
- Minimal change in p99 or throughput on its own. Explanation: MTU helps only if stack produces larger contiguous payloads; fragmentation still occurs at runtime.

B) NIC offload tweaks (disable TSO/GSO, enable Rx coalescing)
- Small improvements in CPU load but inconsistent latency benefits. Disabling TSO sometimes improved tail latency because driver wasn't resegmenting already small sk_buffs, but net effect depended on kernel/OFED version.

C) NCCL algorithm selection (NCCL_ALGO=Ring vs TREE vs COLLNET)
- Ring produced more small messages but consistent latency. Tree reduced number of hops for small collective sizes and improved p99 by ~15% in some workloads. COLLNET had higher memory overhead and mixed results.

D) Application-level coalescing (KV sync batching at runtime): Grouping small KV syncs into a single aggregated message before calling NCCL collective.
- Best single improvement: when runtime batched small syncs into ~32KB messages, we saw the +35% throughput / -36% p99 reduction reported above.

E) Artificial NCCL pacing (spin/sleep between NCCL calls to spread packets in time)
- Introducing micro-pacing (usleep 20–100us) smoothed bursts and reduced instantaneous link saturation. Improved p99 but reduced avg throughput if pacing too aggressive. Optimal pacing around 30–50us in our env.

F) Enabling GDRCopy + UCX tuning (UCX_NET_DEVICES=mlx5_0:1, UCX_RNDV_THRESH=65536)
- GDRCopy reduced CPU overhead at larger message sizes; helpful only combined with batching.

G) Cross-node vs intra-node: Intra-node NVLink transfers not impacted — all problems localized to cross-node NIC path.

Hypotheses validated:
- Root cause is a combination of (a) runtime-level small-message generation pattern (per-token KV sync) and (b) network stack/NCCL behavior that is inefficient for many small RDMA messages.
- Batching/coalescing at the runtime layer gives the best ROI because it avoids touching lower-stack heuristics and reduces total number of NIC interrupts and RDMA operations.

Implementation notes (what we tried in code):
- Introduced a KV-coalescer in the runtime: a loose aggregation window (0–500us) that merges adjacent small sends destined for the same NCCL rank into a single buffer and emits one collective. Controlled via env vars: RI_KV_COALESCE_WINDOW_US, RI_KV_COALESCE_MAX_BYTES.
- Added an adaptive pacing mode: turns on when per-node NIC link utilization > 70% AND average NCCL op size < X (configurable).
- Added metrics: /metrics exposes kv_coalesce_rate, avg_coalesced_bytes, nccl_total_collectives, nccl_avg_payload_size.

Trade-offs and caveats:
- Coalescing increases latency for the very first small packet in a burst by the coalesce window (microseconds). For short-tail latency-sensitive customers we must make window configurable and possibly opt-out per-route.
- Aggressive coalescing interacts poorly with per-request isolation requirements for some privacy-sensitive workloads; need to ensure we don't mix data across tenants. Solution: coalesce only when requests belong to the same tenant and model-version.
- Pacing can mask but not fully solve problems if the underlying algorithm sends many messages because of algorithmic design (e.g., some ring patterns).

Open questions / next steps:
- Is there a way to get NCCL to change its internal message packing for small collective sizes? Explore NCCL patches or contributing a small-message coalesce optimization.
- Could we integrate with UCX to perform application-level coalescing at the transport layer instead of runtime? Trade-offs in complexity.
- How do different NIC vendors/firmware affect optimal windows (we tested only ConnectX-6). Need broader sampling (ConnectX-5/7, Broadcom).
- Does enabling CORNERSTONE (hypothetical kernel NIC aggregation) improve without tuning?

Operational recommendations (short-term):
1) Ship opt-in runtime coalescing (RI_KV_COALESCE_*) behind a feature flag for customers using cross-node tensor parallel configs.
2) Add default UCX env var recommendations to our deployment docs (UCX_RNDV_THRESH, UCX_MAX_RNDV).
3) Provide a diagnostic script pack (tcpdump/tshark capture + simple histograms of packet sizes + NCCL op count) for support to triage.
4) Add a Canary test in Dedicated that runs mixed short/long workloads across nodes and asserts p99 and token/sec thresholds.

Longer-term work:
- Contribute a small-message coalescing path to NCCL/UCX upstream or propose an API for runtimes to hint coalescing semantics.
- Automated tuning: runtime monitors NIC utilization + op size distribution and auto-adjusts coalesce window and pacing in production.
- Benchmark suite: expand our multi-node CI jobs to include small-ops heavy KV-sync patterns across various NICs and firmware versions.

Action items:
- Evan: complete unit tests + integrate coalescer metrics into console dashboard (due 2025-11-18).
- Priya: run vendor matrix (ConnectX-5/6/7 + Broadcom) across our lab and report delta on coalescing effectiveness (due 2025-11-25).
- Liam: draft support diagnostic checklist and the tcpdump parser tool (due 2025-11-11).
- Maya: RFC for opt-in rollout and canary definition (due 2025-11-08).

Appendix: quick commands used during profiling (notes)
- Capture NIC packet sizes: sudo tcpdump -i mlx5_0 -s 0 -w kv-sync.pcap 'port 20000'
- Summarize packets by length: tshark -r kv-sync.pcap -T fields -e frame.len | sort -n | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 50
- NCCL debug env: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL,NET
- UCX tuning: export UCX_RNDV_THRESH=65536 UCX_NET_DEVICES=mlx5_0:1
- Run nsys: nsys profile -o profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --sample=none --duration=60 ./run_infer_bench

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc mixes experimental notes and proposed product changes; please comment on the opt-in default and the telemetry we should add.
- If you have lab access to other NIC vendors, please attach your captures to LLMINF-342.

Unresolved findings we flagged for deeper research:
- Kernel re-segmentation and its interaction with RDMA offloads is surprisingly brittle across OFED versions. We observed opposite effects across two kernels (5.15 vs 6.1).
- NCCL internal batching heuristics are opaque; reaching out to NVIDIA support to ask about recommended flags for high-frequency small collectives.

End.
